summary: `tokio::io::ReadHalf<T>::unsplit` is Unsound
details:
`tokio::io::ReadHalf<T>::unsplit` can violate the `Pin` contract

The soundness issue is described in the [tokio/issues#5372](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/5372)

Specific set of conditions needed to trigger an issue (a !Unpin type in ReadHalf)
is unusual, combined with the difficulty of making any arbitrary use-after-free
exploitable in Rust without doing a lot of careful alignment of data types in
the surrounding code.

The `tokio` feature `io-util` is also required to be enabled to trigger this
soundness issue.

Thanks to zachs18 reporting the issue to Tokio team responsibly and taiki-e
and carllerche appropriately responding and fixing the soundness bug.

Tokio before 0.2.0 used `futures` 0.1 that did not have `Pin`, so it is not
affected by this issue.

summary: atty potential unaligned read
details:
On windows, `atty` dereferences a potentially unaligned pointer.

In practice however, the pointer won't be unaligned unless a custom global allocator is used.

In particular, the `System` allocator on windows uses `HeapAlloc`, which guarantees a large enough alignment.

# atty is Unmaintained

A Pull Request with a fix has been provided over a year ago but the maintainer seems to be unreachable.

Last release of `atty` was almost 3 years ago.

## Possible Alternative(s)

The below list has not been vetted in any way and may or may not contain alternatives;

- [std::io::IsTerminal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html) - Stable since Rust 1.70.0
- [is-terminal](https://crates.io/crates/is-terminal) - Standalone crate supporting Rust older than 1.70.0"

summary: Race Condition Enabling Link Following and Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition in remove_dir_all
details:
The `remove_dir_all` crate is a Rust library that offers additional features over the Rust standard library `fs::remove_dir_all` function. It suffers the same class of failure as the code it was layering over: TOCTOU race conditions, with the ability to cause arbitrary paths to be deleted by substituting a symlink for a path after the type of the path was checked.

Thanks to the Rust security team for identifying the problem and alerting us to it.

summary: Shaman has soundness issues and is unmaintained
details:
`shaman::cryptoutil::write_u64v_le` and other functions mentioned above cannot garantee memory safety of get_unchecked later if both length are zero.

`shaman` is unmaintained.

summary: anon-vec lacks sufficient checks in public API
details:
The following functions in the anon-vec crate are unsound due to insufficient checks on their arguments::

- `AnonVec::get_ref()`
- `AnonVec::get_mut()`
- `AnonVec::remove_get()`

The crate was built as a learning project and is not being maintained.

summary: xous has unsound usages of `core::slice::from_raw_parts`
details:
We consider `as_slice` and `as_slice_mut` unsound because: the pointer with any bit patterns could be cast to the slice of arbitrary types. The pointer could be created by unsafe new and deprecated `from_parts`. We consider that `from_parts` should be removed in latest version because it will help trigger unsoundness in `as_slice`. With new declared as unsafe, `as_slice` should also declared as unsafe.  

This was patched in by marking two functions as `unsafe`.

summary: magic-crypt uses insecure cryptographic algorithms
details:
This crate uses a number of cryptographic algorithms that are no longer considered secure and it uses them in ways that do not guarantee the integrity of the encrypted data.

`MagicCrypt64` uses the insecure DES block cipher in CBC mode without authentication. This allows for practical brute force and padding oracle attacks and does not protect the integrity of the encrypted data. Key and IV are generated from user input using CRC64, which is not at all a key derivation function.

`MagicCrypt64`, `MagicCrypt128`, `MagicCrypt192`, and `MagicCrypt256` are all vulnerable to padding-oracle attacks. None of them protect the integrity of the ciphertext. Furthermore, none use password-based key derivation functions, even though the key is intended to be generated from a password.

Each of the implementations are unsound in that they use uninitialized memory without `MaybeUninit` or equivalent structures.

For more information, visit the [issue](https://github.com/magiclen/rust-magiccrypt/issues/17).

summary: linkme fails to ensure slice elements match the slice's declared type
details:
Affected versions allow populating a DistributedSlice of T with elements of an arbitrary other type that coerces to T. For example, elements of type `&&str` could end up in a slice of type `[&str]`, since `&&str` coerces to `&str` via a deref coercion.

The flaw was corrected by implementing typechecking for distributed slice elements in such a way that coercion no longer occurs. The element's type must be a subtype of the slice's declared element type.

summary: XMP Toolkit's `XmpFile::close` can trigger undefined behavior
details:
Affected versions of the crate failed to catch C++ exceptions raised within the `XmpFile::close` function. If such an exception occurred, it would trigger undefined behavior, typically a process abort.

This is best demonstrated in [issue #230](https://github.com/adobe/xmp-toolkit-rs/issues/230), where a race condition causes the `close` call to fail due to file I/O errors.

This was fixed in [PR #232](https://github.com/adobe/xmp-toolkit-rs/pull/232) (released as crate version 1.9.0), which now safely handles the exception.

For backward compatibility, the existing API ignores the error. A new API `XmpFile::try_close` was added to allow callers to receive and process the error result.

Users of all prior versions of `xmp_toolkit` are encouraged to update to version 1.9.0 to avoid undefined behavior.

summary: Redox UEFI Safe API can cause heap-buffer-overflow
details: ffi::nstr() should be marked unsafe, since a pointer to a buffer without a trailing 0 value will cause a heap buffer overflow.

summary: wrflib has a soundness issue and is unmaintained
details:
All functions under `wrflib::byte_extract` are simply wrapper of unsafe pointer offset and lacks sufficient checks to it pointer and offset parameter.

`wrflib` is unmaintained.

summary: Multiple soundness issues in lexical
details:
`lexical` contains multiple soundness issues:

 1. [Bytes::read() allows creating instances of types with invalid bit patterns](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/102)
 1. [BytesIter::read() advances iterators out of bounds](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/101)
 1. [The `BytesIter` trait has safety invariants but is public and not marked `unsafe`](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/104)
 1. [`write_float()` calls `MaybeUninit::assume_init()` on uninitialized data, which is is not allowed by the Rust abstract machine](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/95)
1. [`radix()` calls `MaybeUninit::assume_init()` on uninitialized data, which is is not allowed by the Rust abstract machine](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/126)

The crate also has some correctness issues.

## Alternatives

For quickly parsing floating-point numbers third-party crates are no longer needed. A fast float parsing algorithm by the author of `lexical` has been [merged](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86761) into libcore.

For quickly parsing integers, consider `atoi` and `btoi` crates (100% safe code). `atoi_radix10` provides even faster parsing, but only with `-C target-cpu=native`, and at the cost of some `unsafe`.

For formatting integers in a `#[no_std]` context consider the [`numtoa`](https://crates.io/crates/numtoa) crate.

For working with big numbers consider `num-bigint` and `num-traits`.

summary: RISC Zero zkVM notes on zero-knowledge
details:
RISC Zero zkVM was designed from its inception to provide three main guarantees:
1. *Computational integrity*: that a given software program executed correctly.
2. *Succinctness*: that the proof of execution does not grow in relation to the program being executed.
3. *Zero Knowledge*: that details of the program execution are not visible within the proof of program execution.

Ulrich Habock and Al Kindi have released [new research] that indicates that several STARK implementations -including our RISC Zero zkVM- do not meet the requirements to assert the specific property of zero knowledge provably. 

While a vast majority of real-world applications that leverage RISC Zero zkVM or similar systems depend primarily on computational integrity and succinctness, a subset of applications critically depend on the privacy guarantees provided by zero-knowledge; and for those use cases, users are cautioned to understand the research and make informed decisions based on the risks outlined in using an impacted system.

Although the maintainers are not aware of any attacks that can take advantage of this potential weakness, they are working to proactively address this discovery as quickly as possible. 

[new research]: https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1037

summary: Ref methods into_ref, into_mut, into_slice, and into_slice_mut are unsound when used with cell::Ref or cell::RefMut
details:
*This advisory is also published as [RUSTSEC-2023-0074](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2023-0074.html).*

The `Ref` methods `into_ref`, `into_mut`, `into_slice`, and `into_slice_mut` are unsound and may allow safe code to exhibit undefined behavior when used with `Ref<B, T>` where `B` is [`cell::Ref`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cell/struct.Ref.html) or [`cell::RefMut`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cell/struct.RefMut.html). Note that these methods remain sound when used with `B` types other than `cell::Ref` or `cell::RefMut`.

See https://github.com/google/zerocopy/issues/716 for a more in-depth analysis.

The current plan is to yank the affected versions soon. See https://github.com/google/zerocopy/issues/679 for more detail.

summary: ferris-says has undefined behavior when not using UTF-8
details:
Affected versions receive a `&[u8]` from the caller through a safe API, and pass it directly to the unsafe `str::from_utf8_unchecked` function.

The behavior of `ferris_says::say` is undefined if the bytes from the caller don't happen to be valid UTF-8.

The flaw was corrected in [ferris-says#21] by using the safe `str::from_utf8` instead, and returning an error on invalid input. However this fix has not yet been published to crates.io as a patch version for 0.2.

Separately, [ferris-says#32] has introduced a different API for version 0.3 which accepts input as `&str` rather than `&[u8]`, so is unaffected by this bug.

[ferris-says#21]: https://github.com/rust-lang/ferris-says/pull/21
[ferris-says#32]: https://github.com/rust-lang/ferris-says/pull/32

summary: Nervos CKB DoS: Process exists when p2p discovery protocol receives unsupported peer IP
details: The p2p discovery protocol assumes that the peer IP must be valid IPv4 address.

summary: dcap-qvl has Missing Verification for QE Identity
details:
## Impact
This vulnerability involves a critical gap in the cryptographic verification process within the dcap-qvl.

The library fetches QE Identity collateral (including qe_identity, qe_identity_signature, and qe_identity_issuer_chain) from the PCCS. However, it skips to verify the QE Identity signature against its certificate chain and does not enforce policy constraints on the QE Report.

## Consequences
An attacker can forge the QE Identity data to whitelist a malicious or non-Intel Quoting Enclave. This allows the attacker to forge the QE and sign untrusted quotes that the verifier will accept as valid. Effectively, this bypasses the entire remote attestation security model, as the verifier can no longer trust the entity responsible for signing the quotes.

## Who is impacted
All deployments utilizing the dcap-qvl library for SGX or TDX quote verification are affected.

## Patches
The vulnerability has been patched in dcap-qvl version 0.3.9. The fix implements the missing cryptographic verification for the QE Identity signature and enforces the required checks for MRSIGNER, ISVPRODID, and ISVSVN against the QE Report.

Users of the `@phala/dcap-qvl-node` and `@phala/dcap-qvl-web` packages should switch to the pure JavaScript implementation, `@phala/dcap-qvl`.

## Workarounds
There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability. Users must upgrade to the patched version to ensure that QE Identity collateral is properly verified.

## Credit
This bug was reported by Rahul Saxena <saxenism@bluethroatlabs.com>.

summary: Rustls: Session Debug formatting exposes TLS master secrets and resumption PSKs
details:
### Summary

Formatting a client session value with Debug exposes its TLS 1.2 master secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK. A custom session store that logs these values can disclose keys to readers of the logs. Ordinary connection and built-in cache diagnostics remain redacted, and the session-store interface already warns that its values are sensitive.

### Details

Derived formatters traverse the session's secret-bearing fields. This conflicts with the project's explicit [key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

### Proof of concept

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations could leak secret data by using the provided `Tls12ClientSessionValue` or `Tls13ClientSessionValue` in a way that triggers its implementation of the `Debug` trait.

### Impact

Such store implementations could leak the master secret for the TLS connection.

### Acknowledgement
Thanks to OpenAI [OutboundDisclosures@openai.com](mailto:OutboundDisclosures@openai.com) for the disclosure.

summary: rustls: An unauthenticated ServerHello poisons the per-name key-exchange record, so later ClientHellos carry only a classical X25519 share
details:
## Summary

The client records the server-selected key-exchange group per server name when it processes the ServerHello, before the server is authenticated. A network attacker can answer one connection attempt for a target name with a ServerHello that selects X25519 and close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that name carry one X25519 share while supported_groups still lists X25519MLKEM768 first. If the server accepts that share instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only and no error.

An attacker that answers one connection attempt for the target name with a ServerHello selecting X25519 changes every later ClientHello of that client for that name, for as long as the entry stays in the store. No certificate or completed handshake is needed: it parses the ClientHello, sends the ServerHello, and closes.

TLS 1.3 transcript binding stops an on-path attacker from editing the ClientHello of one connection. It does not stop the attacker from steering the client's prediction state beforehand, because that state is written from an unauthenticated message.

## What does not trigger it

- Servers that send a HelloRetryRequest. The connection stays hybrid and costs one extra round trip.
- A client configuration with resumption disabled: nothing is stored.
- A different server name: the record is per name.

## Impact

If the genuine server picks the group for which a share is present, instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only, between two peers that both support the hybrid group. No error is raised. The confidentiality of recorded sessions against a future quantum adversary is lost for those connections (harvest now, decrypt later). There is no key compromise and no authentication bypass.

Note that this behaviour is discussed at length in [draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations) so the actual security impact is largely down to a server policy decision.

summary: Rustls: Brotli certificate decompression can allocate an attacker-controlled amount of memory up to 1 GiB before authentication.
details:
### Summary

The built-in (but disabled by default) Brotli certificate decoder bounds the output buffer but accepts an input-selected history window. A header of five bytes can specify a 1 GiB window allocation. A peer can abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request. A client must enable Brotli and connect to the peer; a server must enable Brotli and request a client certificate. Neither direction requires a trusted attacker certificate.

### Details

rustls calls `BrotliDecompress` which enables Brotli's large-window extension. rustls applies a limit to certificates, but this applies to the decompressed result, and not to any internal allocations the process requires.

### Impact

Client applications that enable the `brotli` feature will be vulnerable to malicious servers. Server applications that enable the `brotli` feature and enable client authentication will be vulnerable to malicious clients.

Potential for denial of service due to memory exhaustion from peers sending malicious Brotli-encoded certificates, for applications that enable Brotli decompression.

### Acknowledgement
Thanks to OpenAI [OutboundDisclosures@openai.com](mailto:OutboundDisclosures@openai.com) for the disclosure.

summary: rustls: ECH rejection can expose buffered application data to authenticated outer server before `ech_required` alert
details:
In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of the handshake, `start_traffic()` encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by `ClientConnection::writer()`. It does this *before* checking for `EchStatus::Rejected` and queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application then receives `Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, as expected. However, the client is still expected to call `write_tls()` to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

# Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by `public_name`. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849), which says the following:

- Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert **before sending any application data to the server.**"
- Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against `public_name`, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

- They use `EchMode::Enable`. GREASE ECH is not affected.
- They write application data before the handshake completes.
- They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

summary: Rustls: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries
details:
Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext without rustls rejecting the connection.

This issue affects rustls versions 0.23.13 through 0.23.44 inclusive.

# Original report
### Summary
Rustls (tested version 0.23.44, and it appears still an issue on latest master though I have not tested this) accepts a TLS 1.3 server flight where a plaintext EncryptedExtensions is packed into the same record as the ServerHello.

This is very similar to Go's CVE-2025-61730 fixed in https://github.com/golang/go/commit/5046bdf8a612b35a2c1a9e168054c1d5c65e7dd7

### Details
It appears `Deframer::aligned` considers itself aligned as long as all messages remaining in the buffer are complete. Rustls processes the ServerHello, installs the handshake keys, then pulls the complete (plaintext) EncryptedExtensions out of the buffer.

This is insufficient per RFC 8446 section 5.1's

> Handshake messages MUST NOT span key changes.  Implementations MUST verify that all messages immediately preceding a key change align with a record boundary; if not, then they MUST terminate the connection with an "unexpected_message" alert.  Because the ClientHello, EndOfEarlyData, ServerHello, Finished, and KeyUpdate messages can immediately precede a key change, implementations MUST send these messages in alignment with a record boundary.

### Impact
An on path attacker can inject plaintext messages that are accepted.

### Tool Use Disclosure
This was discovered by a new TLS/DTLS test suite currently under construction. The specific testcase was inspired by the Go CVE. Other tested implementations (Botan, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, Go, wolfSSL) reject this protocol flow. Daybreak Blue reviewed the rustls code to identify probable root cause.

summary: Use-after-free of caller-owned server name in client connection constructors
details:
In rustls-ffi 0.12.0 through 0.15.6, `rustls_client_connection_new()` and
`rustls_client_connection_new_alpn()` retained a reference to the caller's
`server_name` buffer after returning, rather than copying it. The API
documentation did not require the buffer to outlive the call and as a result
if the caller freed or reused the buffer, later TLS processing read freed
memory.

Clients that free or reuse the `server_name` buffer after the constructor
returns are affected. This is most likely for language bindings that pass
temporary strings. Callers that keep the `server_name` buffer alive for the
lifetime of the `rustls_client_config` are not affected.

Versions 0.12.0 through 0.15.6 are affected. Version 0.15.7+ changed these APIs
to copy the input buffer.

summary: Arbitrary code execution when rerunning tests from a portable recording
details:
## Summary

Nextest versions between 0.9.125 and 0.9.149 (inclusive) allow the `cargo nextest run --rerun` (or `-R`) command with a malicious [portable recording](https://nexte.st/docs/features/record-replay-rerun/portable-recordings/) to run arbitrary code during the build. The result is arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running `cargo nextest`.

This vulnerability requires that the experimental [run recording](https://nexte.st/docs/features/record-replay-rerun/) functionality is enabled. An attacker can plausibly trick a victim into enabling this feature.

## Details

Nextest's portable recordings contain [build scope arguments](https://nexte.st/docs/design/architecture/recording-runs/#build-scope-arguments). These arguments are deserialized verbatim from portable recordings, and are [not validated](https://github.com/nextest-rs/nextest/blob/70ba2393a05f29c54b72b4badb9635a86f162eb1/nextest-runner/src/record/format.rs#L421-L426). As a result, it is possible to construct an archive with a custom `--config` argument that causes Cargo to execute arbitrary code.

Nextest 0.9.150 records the build scope as structured data, and passes each value to Cargo joined to its flag (for example, `--package=<value>`), so a recording can no longer add other Cargo options.

## Impact

A malicious portable recording leads to arbitrary code execution as the user who runs `cargo nextest run --rerun`, during the build phase, before any test runs.

- The injected configuration takes effect during `cargo build`, so the payload is run even on a warm build cache, and even when no tests are ultimately executed. Inspecting the recorded tests (with e.g. `cargo nextest replay`) before running them does not help, since the code has already run by the time the tests would start.
- Arbitrary code execution happens as the invoking user, without a prompt or trust warning. The only signal is a `rerun: inheriting build scope…` line. On CI, this includes access to whatever secrets are accessible to the job, including repository tokens and deployment credentials.
- A malicious payload can invoke the real compiler afterwards, so the build and tests complete normally. The recording is otherwise a valid, ordinary recording.
- The full Cargo `--config` surface is exposed. This includes `build.rustc-wrapper`, `build.rustc`, `target.*.linker`, `target.*.runner`, `env.*`, and `patch.*` and `source.*.replace-with` (redirecting dependencies to an attacker-controlled repository or registry).
- The delivery mechanism matches the feature's intended use, since portable recordings are designed to be shared across machines. For example, an attacker could pose as a user asking a maintainer for help triaging their flaky test report. Because `--rerun` also accepts process substitution, `cargo nextest run --rerun <(curl …)` would fetch the recording directly from a URL.

Exploitation requires convincing the victim to run `cargo nextest run --rerun` against an attacker-supplied portable recording. The rerun feature is experimental and must be enabled, via e.g. `NEXTEST_EXPERIMENTAL_RECORD=1`.

## Remediations

- Upgrade cargo-nextest to version 0.9.150 or above.
- In your repositories, set the [minimum required version](https://nexte.st/docs/configuration/minimum-versions/) to 0.9.150. In `.config/nextest.toml`:
  ```toml
  nextest-version = "0.9.150"
  ```
  This way, anyone who interacts with your repository will be notified to upgrade their version of nextest.
- If you are using an affected version, do not enable the experimental run recording feature.

## Credit

Reported by [inanna-malick](https://github.com/inanna-malick).

summary: Use-after-free with `CParameter::StableInBuffer`
details:
With `CParameter::StableInBuffer(true)` (`experimental` feature), the C
library keeps a pointer to the input of one streaming call and reads from it
in later calls, including `flush_stream` and `end_stream`, which take no
input. An `InBuffer` only borrows its slice for one call, so safe code could
free it in between, and freed memory was compressed into the frame. The C
library behaves this way since zstd 1.5.4, whether bundled or linked from the
system.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to enable the parameter.

summary: Uninitialized memory exposed by `write::Decoder` on a corrupt legacy frame
details:
From 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, the writer behind `zstd::stream::write::Decoder` set
its output buffer's length to its full capacity before each decompression
call, then to the position the call reported, and only checked for an error
afterwards. When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7)
frame, the bundled zstd library reports the output as fully written although
nothing was written, so stale heap memory, up to the buffer size (32 KiB by
default), was passed to the wrapped writer.

Legacy support is enabled by default, and a few bytes of corrupt legacy
frame are enough. Whether this reaches an attacker depends on where the
application sends the decompressed output.

From 0.8.0, the writer uses zstd-safe's buffers, and the same flaw there is
covered by the zstd-safe advisory for it, fixed in zstd-safe 8.2.0.

summary: Use-after-free through `init_using_cdict` and `init_using_ddict`
details:
`CCtx::init_using_cdict` and `DCtx::init_using_ddict` (`experimental`
feature, deprecated) took the dictionary as `&CDict<'b>` and `&DDict<'b>`
with only `'b: 'a`, so the dictionary itself could be dropped while the
context still pointed at it. The same mistake in other constructors was
fixed earlier (<https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/365>).

The flaw was corrected by taking `&'a CDict<'b>` and `&'a DDict<'b>`.

summary: `Seekable` reads a NULL or out-of-bounds seek table
details:
`Seekable` did not record whether it was initialized. On a fresh `Seekable`,
or one whose `init_buff()` failed, `decompress`, `offset_to_frame_index` and
`frame_decompressed_size` made the C library read a NULL seek table. After a
failed re-initialization, `decompress` returned data from the refused buffer
using the previous seek table.

Separately, `frame_decompressed_size(num_frames())`, on `Seekable` and
`SeekTable`, read one entry past the end of the seek table.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to use a `Seekable` until an
initialization succeeded, and by checking the frame index.

summary: WebAssembly allocator shim corrupts memory on allocation failure
details:
On wasm32, zstd-sys provides `malloc` and `free` to the C library through a
shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure:
it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C
library used as a valid buffer. `free(NULL)` also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a
small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough)
made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's
linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm
sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size
overflow, and by making `free(NULL)` a no-op.

summary: Aliasing violations in splice, mutable iteration and cursors
details:
Four code paths create a pointer whose permission is later revoked, then
write through it. Miri reports each as undefined behaviour under both the
Tree Borrows and Stacked Borrows aliasing models (CWE-758). All four are
reachable from safe code with standard `Ord` types.

1. **Splice back-pointer.** `split_off`, `split_off_index` and `append` stored
   the first spliced node's `prev` pointer from a reference to the head, then
   wrote through that same reference, invalidating the stored pointer. A later
   `pop_first` or `pop_front` writes through it. This affects all four
   collections.
2. **`SkipMap::range_mut` back pointer.** With an `Included` or `Excluded`
   upper bound, the back pointer came from a shared reference. `next_back`
   hands out `&mut V` through it, and writing to that value is undefined
   behaviour.
3. **`IterMut::next_back` reads a yielded node.** In `SkipList` and `SkipMap`,
   `next_back` read the predecessor node even after the front end had yielded
   it as `&mut`. The read freezes the caller's reference, and the caller's
   next write through it is undefined behaviour. This affects `iter_mut`,
   `values_mut` and `range_mut` used from both ends.
4. **Cursor list pointer.** `lower_bound_mut` and `upper_bound_mut` on
   `OrderedSkipList` and `SkipSet` (`cursor` feature) took the cursor's list
   pointer, then searched through `&self`. A comparator with interior-mutable
   state, such as a `Cell` call counter, wrote to the list's memory through
   that shared borrow and invalidated the cursor's pointer. The comparator can
   be a fully consistent order. `SkipMap` cursors are not affected.

No miscompilation has been observed in an optimised build. A future compiler
may still optimise on the violated aliasing assumptions.

The flaws were corrected in 1.3.0. Each fix derives the pointer used for
mutation from the collection's long-lived allocation pointers, and each has a
Miri regression test.

summary: Uninitialized memory exposed when streaming decompression of a legacy frame fails
details:
When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the
bundled zstd library reports the output buffer as fully written although
nothing was written. `DCtx::decompress_stream` committed that position even
on error, and for a `Vec<u8>` destination this extended the vector's length
over uninitialized memory.

Legacy support is enabled by default. A 5- or 6-byte corrupt legacy frame is
enough: through `zstd::stream::write::Decoder`, up to 32 KiB of stale heap
memory is then passed to the wrapped writer on the next `write()` or
`flush()`, or when an `auto_flush()`/`on_flush()` decoder is dropped. Whether
this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the
decompressed output. `zstd::stream::read::Decoder`, `zstd::decode_all` and
the bulk API are not affected.

Before zstd-safe 4.0.0, output buffers could only be initialized slices.
The zstd crate's own writer had the same flaw from 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, which is
covered by a separate advisory.

The flaw was corrected by only committing the buffer positions of a
successful call.

summary: Use-after-free of a dictionary after a one-shot call on a context with an open stream
details:
The one-shot `DCtx` and `CCtx` methods assumed the C library resets the
context, but it leaves an open stream as it is. When a stream was left
unfinished on a context, a one-shot call such as `decompress_using_dict`
could leave the context pointing at the dictionary borrowed for that call,
and the next streaming call resumed the stream against it after it was
freed: decompressed output then contained freed heap memory. On the
compression side, the stream resumed against the one-shot call's buffers.

This requires an application to use one context for both streaming and
one-shot calls without a reset in between. The flaw was corrected by
resetting the session after one-shot calls whenever a stream may be open.

summary: Build environment compiled into the library and readable at runtime
details:
The build script of `rustpython-vm` 0.3.0 through 0.5.0 writes every
environment variable of the build into `$OUT_DIR/env_vars.rs`. The crate
compiles that file into `_sysconfigdata`'s `build_time_vars`. That module is
always compiled.

A binary built in CI with secrets in the environment carries those secrets
in clear text. Registry tokens, cloud credentials and API keys are the usual
ones. Anyone with the binary can read them with `strings` or from Python.

Version 0.6.0 removes the dump and the include. Users of earlier versions
should upgrade, rebuild, and ship new binaries. Every secret that was in the
environment of a past build whose output left the build machine should be
treated as exposed.

Jacob Finkelman first reported the issue in
[#8802](https://github.com/RustPython/RustPython/issues/8802).
[Bitbison](https://registry.bitbison.io/cargo/rustpython-vm)'s automated
supply chain scanning then detected credential data from the build
environment flowing into artifacts that third-party software ships in the
wild. The leak was confirmed in the published release binaries of at least four
dependants but others have been impacted.

summary: Heap buffer overflow in `CCtx::try_clone` on a multithreaded context
details:
`CCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) copies tables sized
from the context's applied parameters. Starting a multithreaded frame
(`zstdmt` feature) replaces those parameters with the workers' without
resizing the context's own tables, so after an abandoned single-threaded
frame, the copy wrote up to 512 KiB past a heap allocation, or read past
one. This became reachable with the bundled zstd 1.5.6.

The flaw was corrected by refusing `try_clone` (and the unsafe
`compress_block`) once `NbWorkers` was set on the context.

summary: Out-of-bounds read with an out-of-range `InBuffer::pos`
details:
`InBuffer`'s fields are public, so safe code can set `pos` past the end of
`src`. The position was passed to the C library unchecked, and
`ZSTD_seekable_compressStream`, unlike the other streaming functions, does
not validate it: it read past the end of the input slice, by up to the
frame size, and compressed that memory into the output.

The flaw was corrected by checking the position before every call into the
C library.

summary: Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame
details:
When a multithreaded frame (`zstdmt` feature, `CParameter::NbWorkers`) is
left unfinished, its jobs may still be running on the worker threads: the C
library only waits for them when the next frame starts, or when the context
is freed. A session reset makes the context accept changes again in the
meantime, so:

- unloading the dictionary (`load_dictionary`, `ref_cdict`, `ref_prefix`,
  `disable_dictionary`, `init*`, or `reset` with parameters) freed the
  dictionary a worker was still compressing against;
- changing `NbWorkers` made the next frame resize the job table before
  waiting for the old jobs.

The flaw was corrected by refusing these calls while a multithreaded frame
is unfinished. The new `CCtx::wait_for_workers()` waits for the workers
first.

summary: Double free in `DCtx::try_clone`
details:
`DCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) is a plain copy of the
C context. A context owning a dictionary (from `load_dictionary`,
`ref_prefix` or `init_using_dict`) or a dictionary table (`ref_ddict` with
`RefMultipleDDicts`) ended up with both copies freeing it. A context cloned
mid-frame resumed on uninitialized stream state. The clone also silently lost
the `WindowLogMax` limit.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to clone such contexts, and by carrying
over the parameters the copy leaves out.

summary: `Seekable::decompress` sets a `Vec` length beyond its capacity for offsets past the end
details:
`ZSTD_seekable_decompress` shortens the requested length to the end of the
data without checking that the offset is before it. For an offset past the
end, it returns a wrapped-around length without writing anything, and
`Seekable::decompress` passed that length to `Vec::set_len`.

With the `seekable` feature, whoever supplies the archive, or chooses the
offset, can leave the caller's `Vec<u8>` with a length far beyond its
capacity. Reading it then discloses neighbouring heap memory, and appending
to it corrupts memory. Offsets near `u64::MAX` can also hang the call.

The flaw was corrected by clamping requests to the end of the data, and by
checking every count reported by the C library against the buffer capacity.

summary: Out-of-bounds read in `Log2Cache::nlog2n()`, `nlog2n_difference()` and `plog2p()`
details:
`Log2Cache::new(n)` fills its three tables with entries for `0..=n`, but the
three accessor methods index those tables with `get_unchecked` on a value the
caller supplies. Nothing bounds the argument and nothing documents a bound, so
any value above the `n` the cache was built with reads past the end of the
vector. `CountType` is `u32`, so the read can land up to `u32::MAX` elements
away, and `plog2p()` returns the value it read, disclosing whatever lies there.

For example, `Log2Cache::new(4)` builds tables holding 5 entries (indices
0,1,2,3,4). Then `cache.nlog2n(60000)` reads index 60000, far outside the
allocation. Under AddressSanitizer this faults with `SEGV`; Miri reports it as
undefined behavior at `src/log2cache.rs:42`.

`nlog2n_difference()` is off by one further: in the affected versions `new(n)`
pushes `n` entries into that table rather than `n + 1`, so even
`nlog2n_difference(n)` is out of bounds.

This can be triggered through safe public APIs — `Log2Cache::new()` and any of
`nlog2n()`, `nlog2n_difference()` and `plog2p()` — with no `unsafe` required
from the caller.

summary: `OutBuffer::around_pos` exposes uninitialized memory
details:
`OutBuffer::around_pos` accepted a position past the initialized length of a
`Vec<u8>`. The next streaming call then marked everything before the
position as initialized, so safe code could read stale heap memory between
the vector's previous length and that position.

The flaw was corrected by zero-filling that gap.

summary: Data from an abandoned stream leaks into the next stream on a reused context
details:
The `with_context` constructors of the stream encoders and decoders used the
borrowed context as it was. When a stream was abandoned on a context, for
example an encoder dropped before `finish()` after an error, whatever it
left there was carried into the next stream: the input buffered by the
previous encoder (up to 128 KiB, or all of it with `zstdmt`) became the
start of the next frame, and a decoder returned undelivered output of the
previous stream.

An application reusing one context for data that must stay separate, such
as different users' requests, could disclose one user's plaintext to
another. Whoever supplies the data can cause the abandonment with invalid
input.

The flaw was corrected by resetting the context's session in
`with_context`.

summary: Out-of-bounds read when training a dictionary from inconsistent sample sizes
details:
`ZDICT_trainFromBuffer` is never told the length of the samples buffer.
Before 0.4.10, `zstd::dict::from_continuous` (initially `train_dict`) called
it directly: up to 0.2.1 without checking the sample sizes against the
buffer at all, and from 0.3.0 with a sum that wraps around when overflow
checks are off, as in release builds. Sizes that do not describe the buffer
made the trainer read past its end.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. From
0.4.10, training goes through zstd-safe, where the same flaw is covered by
the zstd-safe advisory for it, fixed in zstd-safe 8.2.0.

summary: SSRF and local file disclosure via unvalidated URLs
details:
Applications that pass attacker-controlled URLs to `webpage` versions before
2.1.0 may be vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF) or local file
disclosure.

`HTTP::fetch` and `Webpage::from_url` passed URLs to libcurl without
restricting the URL scheme or validating the resolved destination IP address.
Redirects were followed without checking whether the new destination was
internal. Depending on how the application uses the response, an attacker
could:

- Read local files accessible to the application process using `file://` URLs.
- Cause requests to internal or link-local services (e.g. cloud metadata
  endpoints at `http://169.254.169.254`) via direct private-IP URLs or by
  chaining HTTP redirects through an attacker-controlled server.

Starting in 2.1.0, `HTTP::fetch` and `Webpage::from_url` reject non-HTTP(S)
URL schemes and destinations that resolve to non-public IP addresses, including
after redirects. Applications that intentionally fetch trusted internal
resources can opt in to the previous behavior with `HTTP::fetch_unrestricted`
or `Webpage::from_url_unrestricted`.

Reported by [Aiden Mohan](https://github.com/AidenMohan).

summary: Use-after-free from a comparator that answers inconsistently
details:
`OrderedSkipList`, `SkipSet` and `SkipMap` can free a node that is still
linked when a `Comparator` or `Ord` implementation gives different answers for
the same pair of values during one mutating call. A later call reads the freed
memory (CWE-416). A safe `impl Ord` with the default comparator is enough to
reach it.

The mutating traversals record a precursor at each level: the last node whose
link points at a node comparing not-`Less` than the target. The splice code
assumes every recorded precursor's link points at or past the final position.
If a later comparison reports one of those nodes as `Less`, the walk steps
past it and the assumption breaks. Removals such as `take_first`, `take` and
`remove` then rewire the wrong link and free the target while its real
predecessor still points at it. `insert` builds crossed links and wrong skip
distances from the same precursors.

A comparator that is a pure function of its two arguments cannot trigger
this, even if it is not transitive. The trigger is a stateful or
non-deterministic implementation, for example one that reads a counter, a
cache, a clock or a random source.

The flaw was corrected in 1.3.0. The mutating traversals track the link target
of the lowest recorded precursor and panic with "comparator does not implement
a total order" when a `Less` answer contradicts an earlier one. Every splice
site also checks its precursors before the first write. Each detected
contradiction panics before any link, value or length changes, so the
collection stays valid and safe to drop.

summary: `PamHandle::get_user` can cause an authentication bypass
details:
In affected versions, `PamHandle::get_user` can return `Err(PAM_SUCCESS)` after it gets the username successfully.
PAM modules that return this "error" code from `sm_authenticate` or `sm_acct_mgmt` early-return a success code to PAM without doing any further verification.
This means a user could log in when they shouldn't be able to (e.g., if the module is `sufficient`).

The `pam_try!` macro of this crate early-returns the code in this exact way:

```rust
fn sm_authenticate(pamh: &mut PamHandle, args: Vec<&CStr>, flags: PamFlag) -> PamResultCode {
    let user = pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None)); // Can return PAM_SUCCESS here.
    // If it does, the module does not get to this line.
}
```

The root cause is an [incorrect FFI declaration][ffi-decl] for [`pam_get_user(3)`][pam-get-user].
This C function writes a pointer to the username through its `user` argument (of type `const char **user`).
This crate's binding declared this argument as a shared reference (`&*mut c_char`).
Writing through a shared reference is [undefined behavior][ub-immutable].

Thus, the compiler can assume that the local pointer, whose address is passed as `user`, is still null after the call.
After the call, the affected code [returns `Ok`][null-check] only if the return code is `PAM_SUCCESS` *and* this pointer is not null.
Otherwise, it returns the return code as an error.
If the compiler assumes that the pointer is null, `get_user` returns an error even when the return code is `PAM_SUCCESS`.
Release builds have been [observed to do this][observed-irl].
Debug builds usually work correctly, so tests in debug mode can miss the problem.

Version 0.1.2 changes the declaration to `&mut *const c_char`.
The fix is in commit [401c961](https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/commit/401c961800c4dde356464b6a7d455af844a3954a).

If a module cannot upgrade, do not return the error code from `get_user`.
Return a failure code instead, for example `pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None), PamResultCode::PAM_AUTH_ERR)`.
This makes the module deny access instead of allowing it, but the undefined behavior remains.

[pam-get-user]: https://github.com/linux-pam/linux-pam/blob/28fce1fd55b003fec90f34e5bc785e9439b216f2/libpam/include/security/pam_modules.h#L30-L31
[ffi-decl]: https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/blob/3d9318b5b812d9142595928deec23e5843a60995/pam/src/module.rs#L49-L53
[ub-immutable]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html#r-undefined.immutable
[null-check]: https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/blob/3d9318b5b812d9142595928deec23e5843a60995/pam/src/module.rs#L196-L202
[observed-irl]: https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/issues/16#issuecomment-3693665220

summary: Out-of-bounds read in `train_from_buffer` when sample sizes overflow
details:
`ZDICT_trainFromBuffer` is never told the length of the samples buffer, so
`train_from_buffer` checked that the sample sizes add up to it. With
overflow checks off, as in release builds, that sum wrapped around: sizes
totalling 2^64 plus the buffer length passed the check, and the trainer read
past the end of the buffer. `zstd::dict::from_continuous` relies on this
check from zstd 0.4.10; older versions of zstd had their own, covered by a
separate advisory.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. The flaw
was corrected by summing the sizes with overflow checks.

summary: Pingora HTTP/2 :authority and Host header mismatch enables cache poisoning and host-based access control bypass
details:
Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 accepted HTTP/2 requests whose Host header differed from the `:authority` pseudo-header. Request filters, cache keys, and logs that read the request URI (`session.req_header().uri`) saw the `:authority` value, but the upstream received the client-supplied Host value. Pingora also accepted `:authority` values containing userinfo (for example, `user@example.com`). This violates RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1, which requires an intermediary to use the `:authority` value for Host and replace any existing Host field.

A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a single HTTP/2 request that the application sees as one host and the upstream receives as another. Where request filters, access controls, or cache keys use the URI authority and the upstream routes by Host, this can lead to cache poisoning, where a response from another virtual host is stored under the victim host's cache key and served to other users, or host-based access control bypass, where a request approved for one host is served by a different virtual host on the upstream. Deployments that do not accept HTTP/2 from clients, or that do not use the request authority for security or caching decisions, are not affected.

This flaw was corrected in commits 915590a91811877795531f6ba0927a3138b5cb4b and ffab8302d08d4292d1924eb8fe84647fd5cb8e76. Pingora now returns 400 Bad Request for HTTP/2 requests whose Host differs from `:authority`, that contain more than one Host, or whose authority contains userinfo, and keeps the upstream Host or `:authority` consistent with the request authority. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.9.0.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.

summary: Pingora forwards client-nominated Connection headers to HTTP/1 upstreams, allowing ACL bypass in specific chained deployments
details:
Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 passed the downstream request through `upstream_request_filter` and wrote it to HTTP/1 upstreams without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominated, although RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1 requires intermediaries to remove them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers. A client could therefore nominate a header that the application adds in `upstream_request_filter` (for example, `Connection: keep-alive, X-Forwarded-For`). A downstream HTTP/1 intermediary that honors Connection would then strip the Pingora-added header before it reached the origin.

This specifically affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin processes Connection nominations (for example, Go's `net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy`) and the origin trusts headers added by that intermediary (for example, X-Forwarded-For for IP-based authorization). A remote, unauthenticated attacker can have those headers removed, potentially bypassing authorization. This is the same class of issue as CVE-2022-31813 in Apache HTTP Server.

This flaw was corrected in commits 28c18e6b6b04dd0bd937234e5950049e6d74cded and ca23f1668eca8e78be7ba62ef0edbd458b40eeee. By default, Pingora now removes hop-by-hop and Connection-nominated headers from upstream requests, and rejects requests whose Connection header nominates Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, or a pseudo-header. This is controlled by `PeerOptions::http_upstream_request_policy`; `HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy::preserve()` restores the old passthrough behavior and should not be used if the origin relies on headers added by Pingora. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.9.0.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as no such chained deployment as described above exists with internal Pingora services, and Connection headers are sanitized before arriving at Pingora gateways.

summary: Pingora HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion through unbounded default header-list and concurrent-stream limits
details:
Pingora versions prior to 0.8.1 used the h2 crate's default HTTP/2 server limits, a 16 MiB decoded header-list size and no limit on concurrent streams, unless the application set its own. A remote, unauthenticated client can send 1-byte HPACK references to a near-empty header, making the server allocate hundreds of thousands of header fields per stream across an unlimited number of streams on one connection, and use HTTP/2 flow control to keep those streams open. This can exhaust memory and degrade or terminate the Pingora process.

This affects any Pingora service that terminates HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) without explicitly setting `max_header_list_size` and `max_concurrent_streams`. The reporter showed that a single connection could get a Pingora process with a 2 GiB memory limit OOM-killed.

This flaw was corrected in commit d193c8d49b8b7c1c1ede93183759caa4f6906bbd. When no `H2Options` are supplied, Pingora now advertises and enforces a 64 KiB decoded header-list limit and at most 100 concurrent streams per connection. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.8.1. Applications that supply their own `H2Options` are not covered by these defaults and must set `max_header_list_size` and `max_concurrent_streams` explicitly, or start from `pingora_core::protocols::http::v2::server::default_h2_options()`. `H2Options::default()` does not include these limits.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.

summary: Race condition in `tokio::time::Interval` on Tokio v1.54.0
details:
## Summary

On the multi-threaded runtime, there is a race condition between `Interval::poll_tick` and the runtime's time driver.

This affects `Interval` only. `Sleep` and `Timeout` are **not** affected.

## Details

In Tokio v1.54.0, a race condition between `tokio::time::Interval::poll_tick` (including `.tick().await`) and the runtime time driver can drop an internal timer entry without synchronizing with the driver thread that is firing it. This causes a data race and use-after-free on the timer's waker and task state in safe Rust, leading to assertion panics, task reference-count corruption, or heap memory corruption.

This bug was introduced by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8458, and it was fixed by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8692.

## Impact

This may lead to crashes and use-after-frees in applications using `Interval` on a multi-threaded runtime.

Since this issue is known to lead to crashes in production systems, the v1.54.0 release of Tokio has been yanked.

## Credits

Thank you to [creepycode](https://github.com/ByteZ1337) and [carabistouille](https://github.com/carabistouflette) for reporting this privately using the procedure outlined in our security policy. They both reported the issue independently of each other.
